newsitem.title: FRANCE: France weighs action against far-rightist Le Pen.
newsitem.headline: France weighs action against far-rightist Le Pen.

text.p: French Justice Minister Jacques Toubon on Thursday weighed legal action against far-right leader Jean-Marie Le Pen after his espousal of racial inequality, ministerial aides said.
"We are in the process of assessing the matter," said one Toubon aide, who spoke on condition of anonymity.

"I think the justice minister will be weighing, word by word, the statements of Mr Le Pen which break the law," said Eric Raoult, junior minister for territorial planning, urban affairs and integration.
Inciting racial hatred is a crime in France, punishable by up to a year in prison, fines of up to 300,000 francs ($60,000) and five years' ineligibility for public office.
Raoult, speaking on France Inter radio, said Le Pen was "turning into a Nazi" while his National Front party "has become fascist".

Numerous human rights organisations and political leaders, most from the opposition Left, have advocated banning Le Pen's National Front or taking it to court since Le Pen's remarks that inequality between races was "a fact".
Toubon on Wednesday had appeared to dismiss opposition appeals for legal action against Le Pen, saying only that it was up to individual politicians to condemn his remarks.
But Defence Minister Charles Millon said on Thursday that France should use all available legal weapons against the outspoken far-right politician.
"Can one say with impunity that human beings do not have equal rights and dignity?" Millon asked on RTL radio.
"If our current legal and judicial arsenal is inadequate, then parliament must take up this matter," Millon added.
An unrepentant Le Pen said in a television interview on Wednesday, "I don't see why saying one does not believe in racial equality is a violation of human dignity."
"I will not be intimidated by the demonstrations or the threats of a 'thought police'," he told LCI television.
The controversy came amid discussion of election law reforms expected to help the Front break into the National Assembly, where it now has no seats, in the 1998 general elections.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe had last week proposed a reform in election law that political analysts said would enable the Front to win a sizeable bloc of seats in the National Assembly.

A major goal of the reforms appeared to be an attempt at winning goodwill from Le Pen, who has routinely opposed all the ruling centre-right's candidates, even when a Front candidate was not in the race.
The centre-right is worried that the anti-immigrant National Front could take enough votes from it in 1998 to hand control of parliament to the Left, which governed until 1993.

Le Pen, whose slogan is "France for the French" and who once dismissed Nazi gas chambers as "a mere detail in the history of World War Two", won 15 percent of the vote in last year's presidential elections.
